source.title: Pre-Trained Policy Discriminators are General Reward Models
source.authors: Shi-Han Dou; Shichun Liu; Yuming Yang; Yicheng Zou; Yunhua Zhou; Shu-Hao Xing; Chen-Hao Huang; Qi-Ming Ge; Hai-Jun Lv; De-Min Song; Song-Yang Gao; Chengqi Lyu; En-Yu Zhou; Honglin Guo; Zhi-Heng Xi; Qi-Peng Guo; Wen-Wei Zhang; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xipeng Qiu; Xuan-Jing Huang; Kai Chen

record.file_problem: Minor PDF text and notation garbling; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends scaling-law experiments to pre-trained reward models, reporting validation-loss trends against parameter count and training compute.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling results concern POLAR reward-model validation loss, not held-out next-token cross-entropy for language models. They therefore do not test V1 or V2 as stated. The paper reports no fixed-compute parameter/token allocation optimum. Preference-evaluation and RLHF benchmark results are not rows for these versions. Hyperparameter fits are described as a way to select learning rate and batch size, not as results on the claim.
record.test_reason: It fits validation loss against parameters and compute for a new training regime: POLAR reward-model pre-training with a Bradley-Terry policy-discrimination objective, starting from pre-trained LMs. Its own results bear on whether the power-law form carries over to other regimes (V5). It does not measure next-token LM loss, so V1 and V2 are not tested as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that POLAR reward models show clear power-law scaling of validation loss with model size and compute, similar to LLMs, suggesting that further scaling will improve reward models.
record.recipe_differences: This is reward-model pretraining using policy-discrimination training and validation loss, rather than language-model next-token pretraining loss. The models are initialized from pre-trained InternLM2.5 models.

fits_no_version.finding: Moving the reward model from POLAR-1.8B to POLAR-7B barely changes preference accuracy (74.0% vs 76.3% on average). It does raise downstream RLHF policy averages, e.g. Llama-3.1-8B goes from 52.71 to 56.33. This is only a two-point comparison of reward-model scale against policy outcomes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-model scale improves downstream RLHF policy performance more than it improves preference-benchmark accuracy.

record.problems: The scaling experiment covers five reward models from 50M to 1B parameters and up to 54B training tokens. Raw data points and error bars are not stated in the text. The fit coefficients in the text differ from the coefficients displayed in Figure 4, although the exponents and R² values match.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows. Preference-evaluation, RLHF, and ablation results do not measure the scaling behaviors named by the tested version.

untested.parts: Held-out next-token pretraining loss of language models versus N, D or C.
Extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs. The paper only asserts that this is possible.
Effects of model shape at fixed parameter count.
Loss versus data size D, which is not fitted separately. Also untested: image, video and other modalities, repeated data, and other fine-tuning regimes.
Downstream task predictability of language models from scale or loss.
Sensitivity of exponents to fitting or setup choices, and curvature away from a power law.

record.verdict_notes: The hyperparameter scaling fits (learning rate and batch size against N, Dp, Drm; Appendix D.1.2) are used to select settings and are correctly excluded as rows. The paper is not an original source. The small exponents and narrow parameter range limit how much weight the V5 support carries.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small language-model runs predict substantially larger runs.
The fixed-compute loss-minimising allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes beyond the tested POLAR reward-model setting, including image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with fitting choices or setup, or curves bend from a power law.

rows.subject: POLAR reward models
rows.size_stated: Five models ranging from 50M to 1B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Trained reward models at different parameter counts and fitted validation loss against model parameters.
rows.note: The text reports a power-law fit across five reward-model sizes. Figure 4's plotted fit label instead shows L = 20.9 N^-0.0425.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. Caveats: only five model sizes over about 1.3 orders of magnitude (50M–1B). There is no irreducible-loss term, and raw points are not tabulated. The coefficient differs between the text (0.9) and Figure 4 (20.9). The text implies scaling-run models start from pre-trained base models, so this is continued training or transfer, not from-scratch pre-training.

rows.subject: POLAR reward models
rows.size_stated: Five models ranging from 50M to 1B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Tracked validation loss during training at different compute levels and fitted loss against optimal training compute.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus optimal training compute
rows.note: The text reports a power-law fit. Figure 4's plotted fit label instead shows L = 22.4 C^-0.0342. This is not a test of a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. This is a frontier fit of loss against compute over training curves (about 10^18–10^21 on the axis), not a compute-optimal N/D allocation. The coefficient differs between the text (2.4) and Figure 4 (22.4).

relationships.condition: POLAR reward-model pre-training (BT policy-discrimination loss), 50M–1B parameters, up to 54B tokens
relationships.reason: Validation loss fits power laws in N (exponent −0.0425, R²=0.9886) and in compute (exponent −0.0342, R²=0.9912) (r1, r2). The size range is narrow and only five points are used.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss fitted parameter scaling with exponent −0.0425 and R²=0.9886, and compute scaling with exponent −0.0342 and R²=0.9912, using five measurements.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
